summary: A country on the Atlantic coast of West Africa that includes the Bijagós Islands; it was a Portuguese colony and declared independence in 1973, and cashew nuts are its most important export.

ranking.name: Islam
ranking.description: Islam is followed mainly by the Fula and Mandinka of the east. From the 13th century the Mandinka founded the Kingdom of Kaabu here as part of the Mali Empire; in the 19th century the Fula Islamic state of Futa Jallon gradually expanded and defeated the Kingdom of Kaabu at the Battle of Kansala in 1867, making Islam the mainstream in the east around Gabú and Bafatá. In recent years the proportion of Muslims has risen through population growth and conversion and is now close to half.

ranking.name: Traditional beliefs
ranking.description: The Balanta, Papel, Manjaco and the inhabitants of the Bijagós Islands on the coast have long preserved ancestral and spirit worship, making offerings at "iran" shrines. These peoples resisted Islamization, and the Portuguese did not truly complete their "pacification" conquest until the 1930s, so traditional beliefs have continued to this day, and the Bijagós Islands still preserve matrilineal society and the tradition of priestesses.

ranking.name: Christianity
ranking.description: Portuguese navigators first reached the coast here in 1446 and established a trading post at Cacheu in 1588, and Catholicism spread among the Creole-speaking mixed-race and urban population. During the colonial period Portuguese influence in the interior was limited, and Catholicism has always been centered on towns such as Bissau and Cacheu; in recent years evangelical churches have also grown among young people.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: The non-religious are found mostly in the capital Bissau, influenced by urban life and education. Because traditional beliefs are still common in daily life, the proportion of people who identify with no religion at all is not high.

religion.background: Guinea-Bissau lies at the boundary between the Mandinka Kingdom of Kaabu and the coastal peoples; the east was gradually Islamized from the Middle Ages, while the coastal peoples long maintained their traditional beliefs. After the Portuguese arrived in the mid-15th century they established bases on the coast for the slave and commodity trade, bringing Catholicism, but they did not control the interior until the early 20th century. After the war of independence of 1963–1974 led by Amílcar Cabral, the country adopted a secular system, resulting in a three-way division among Islam, traditional beliefs and Christianity.

ranking.name: Guinea-Bissau Creole (Kriol)
ranking.description: Guinea-Bissau Creole is based on Portuguese and formed in the 16th–17th centuries at trading posts such as Cacheu, from communication between Portuguese traders, mixed-race residents and Africans of various peoples. During the war of independence of 1963–1974 the African Party for the Independence of Guinea and Cape Verde (PAIGC) used Creole to unite the different peoples, making it a symbol of national identity. Today it is the lingua franca of the whole country, and most people can speak it.

ranking.name: Fula
ranking.description: Fula is the language of the Fula people of the east; the Fula were originally nomadic people who entered the area in the 19th century with the expansion of the Islamic power of Futa Jallon, and became one of the main peoples in regions such as Gabú and Bafatá.

ranking.name: Portuguese
ranking.description: Portugal was active on the coast from the 15th century, formally colonized the country in the late 19th century, and recognized its independence in 1974. Portuguese is the official language, used in government, education and the media, but only a small urban elite have it as a mother tongue, and most people use Creole or their ethnic languages in daily life.

language.history: Guinea-Bissau has more than twenty ethnic groups, and their languages mostly belong to the Atlantic and Mande branches of the Niger–Congo family, such as Balanta, Fula, Mandinka and Papel. After the Portuguese arrived in the 15th century, a Portuguese-based Creole formed at the coastal trading posts, closely related to Cape Verdean Creole. During the colonial period Portuguese was the official and educational language, while the war of independence raised the status of Creole, making it the national lingua franca across ethnic lines.

ranking.name: Palm fruit soup (chabéu)
ranking.description: A thick orange-red soup boiled from palm fruit (chabéu), stewed with fish, shrimp or chicken, and eaten with white rice.
ranking.history: The oil palm is native to West Africa and has been an important source of fat and food there for thousands of years, and the coastal and forest regions of Guinea-Bissau abound in palm fruit. "Chabéu" is the Creole word for palm fruit, and this soup is regarded as the national dish of Guinea-Bissau, always appearing at weddings, festivals and when hosting guests, reflecting the local food tradition based on rice and palm fruit.

ranking.name: Peanut stew
ranking.description: Chicken or fish stewed with peanut butter, tomato and onion in a thick, rich sauce with a nutty sweet aroma, eaten with white rice; a common home dish.
ranking.history: "Mancarra" is the Creole word for peanut. Peanuts are native to South America, were introduced to West Africa by the Portuguese in the 16th century, and were grown for export as a cash crop in Guinea-Bissau in the colonial period. This peanut stew is similar to the peanut stews found throughout West Africa and is an everyday dish in Guinea-Bissau households.

ranking.name: Tomato rice with meat
ranking.description: Red rice cooked with tomato, onion and oil, often cooked together with chicken, fish or vegetables; the grains absorb the sauce and become richly fragrant.
ranking.history: The Balanta of coastal Guinea-Bissau are skilled at building dikes in mangrove swamps to grow rice, developing a long-established technique of rice cultivation, so rice is the country's most important staple. This rice dish originates from the jollof rice of the Wolof of Senegambia, came with regional trade, and is often made at festivals and gatherings.

ranking.name: Yassa (lemon-onion chicken)
ranking.description: Chicken or fish is marinated in plenty of onion, lemon juice and mustard, grilled, and then stewed with the onion sauce; the flavor is rich and tangy, and it is eaten with white rice.
ranking.history: Yassa originates in the Casamance region of northern neighboring Senegal, and before the late 19th century Casamance was part of the Portuguese sphere of influence, with close ethnic and cultural ties to Guinea-Bissau. The dish is therefore very common in Guinea-Bissau and is often seen in homes and restaurants.

ranking.name: Cashew
ranking.description: The fruit of the cashew tree, whose kernel is crunchy and delicious when roasted; the red-yellow cashew apple attached above the nut can be eaten fresh or made into fruit wine.
ranking.history: The cashew tree is native to Brazil and was introduced to Africa by the Portuguese in the 16th century. From the late 20th century cashew nuts became Guinea-Bissau's most important export, accounting for the vast majority of export value, and a large proportion of households across the country depend on growing and harvesting cashews for their livelihood. In the harvest season each year people also make fruit wine and distilled spirits from cashew apples, and the price of cashews even affects the national economy and political stability.
